messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 61
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Bus Driver
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 37

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Visual/Bodily Cues: Blood, Loss of Control: Lack of control, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
  Maladaptive Strategies: Magical Prevention: perform mental rituals to prevent bad things from happening again, Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others, Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
  Memory: Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
  Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Vignette:
Elena, a 61-year-old bus driver for a municipal transit authority, still sees the man’s face when she closes her eyes. The accident happened two years ago, just after she’d pulled her bus away from a downtown stop. A car ran a red light and struck a pedestrian crossing the street. Elena watched the whole thing from her elevated seat—the man’s body folding, the blood pooling on the asphalt, the driver who did not stop. She remembers screaming into her radio for help, but no one came quickly enough. The man died before the paramedics arrived. She has not forgiven herself. She was certain that if she had jumped out of her bus sooner, if she had run into the street and somehow stopped the car, the outcome would have been different. She will never forgive herself for not doing more, and the thought that she should have protected a stranger—a failure she replays daily—has hollowed out the life she used to know.

In the months afterward, Elena began to notice that certain things would pull her back into that moment without warning. The sight of blood, even a small cut on her own hand, makes her stomach clench and her vision narrow. When she drives her route and sees a car hit another car, or merely hears the screech of brakes, her whole body goes rigid—she tastes metal, hears the man’s final breath, smells the hot asphalt. These episodes are not simply memories; they are complete relivings where the event feels present, not past. Sometimes the emotional storm arrives without any image at all—she will be standing in her kitchen and suddenly feel the full weight of helplessness and horror, even though no picture comes to mind. What she had not fully anticipated was how strongly a loss of control would trigger her. Being a passenger in her husband’s car, for instance, sends her heart racing because she cannot stop or steer. When traffic forces her to idle at an intersection near the accident site, the helplessness rises like a wave—the same helplessness she felt watching the man die, unable to intervene, unable to change a single thing. At work, if a passenger insists on standing by the front doors or lingers too long in the aisle, she feels a sudden, suffocating loss of control over her space; the man’s face flashes before her, and she has to grip the wheel to keep from shaking.

To manage this, Elena has developed a set of private rituals. If she passes a spot where something bad could happen, she repeats a phrase under her breath five times—something her grandmother used to say about protection. She counts the seconds between red lights, and if the number lands on an unlucky integer, she starts over. She is certain that if she performs these mental routines correctly, she can prevent another accident from occurring. At the same time, she has begun to avoid any physical contact with passengers or coworkers. She does not shake hands, she angles her body away when someone reaches for a fare, and she flinches if her husband touches her unexpectedly in bed. Grief reminders are even harder: she cannot look at photographs of anyone who has died, including her own mother, because the pain of that loss merges with the guilt of the stranger’s death and becomes unbearable. Her husband has grown bewildered and hurt by her withdrawal. Their marriage, once warm, now operates at a careful distance.

At work, the consequences have accumulated. Elena used to enjoy the camaraderie of the depot, but now she eats lunch alone in her bus so no one will sit too close. She has asked to switch routes three times, trying to avoid intersections where she might see a crash, but there is no route in the city free of traffic. Her supervisor has noticed her jumpiness and has questioned her reliability. Elena does not tell anyone about the rituals or the flashbacks. She is not sure her life is worth living anymore—the weight of the guilt has made her wonder if continuing is even worthwhile. What finally brought her to seek help was a day last week when a child stumbled and scraped his knee on the sidewalk near her bus. The blood sent her into a full sensory reliving, and she had to pull over, shaking and crying, unable to drive for twenty minutes. The dispatch had to send a replacement. She was terrified that someone would see her as unstable, that she would lose her job, that the failure to protect would be exposed. She came to the clinic hoping to quiet the rituals and the memories, but what she is most afraid of is that the guilt will never lift—that she will always be the woman who sat still while someone died, and that no amount of counting or repeating will ever make it right.
